Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 benchmarks with strong results (96.7% AUROC on MVTec-AD), extensive ablations (Table A4), and per-category performance analysis
Practical training-free approach requiring only a frozen encoder, addressing a real limitation of existing methods that need labeled anomaly-free data
Well-motivated methodology with clear three-stage pipeline combining multi-layer feature extraction, global context retrieval, and spatial-conditioned patch matching
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details in Appendix A, hyperparameter specifications, and supporting qualitative visualizations across datasets
weaknesses: Restrictive theoretical assumptions (Assumption 2.1-2.2) that may not hold universally; limited empirical validation that assumptions actually hold for the experimental setup
Critical practical considerations unaddressed: no latency measurements, memory requirements not quantified, and scalability to large datasets unclear despite being key deployment concerns
Limited method novelty: memory bank approaches and retrieval-based scoring are well-established; primary contribution is application to training-free MUAD rather than novel techniques
No statistical significance testing across multiple runs; improvements often modest (<1-2%); unclear if reported differences are statistically significant or reproducible
Heavy dependency on strong frozen encoder (DiNOv3) with significant performance variance across encoders (98.5% vs 96.0%); limited guidance for encoder selection in new domains
Performance degrades substantially under data scarcity (Section 5.4: τ=0.05 ratio shows significant drops) with no clear guidance on minimum normal sample requirements
Cold-start scalability concern: at τ=0.05, the method becomes suboptimal; unclear when the approach is practically applicable with limited normal samples

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on four major benchmarks with multiple metrics (image-level and pixel-level), supplemented by ablation studies that clearly decompose component contributions
Strong and consistent empirical results, particularly in few-shot and data-scarce scenarios, with competitive pixel-level localization performance across MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM
Rigorous theoretical analysis of the fidelity-stability dilemma in reconstruction-based MUAD methods, with detailed mathematical derivations (Assumptions 2.1, Lemmas 2.1-2.2) in appendices
Practical value from training-free deployment: given a frozen encoder, the method naturally handles new anomaly classes without task-specific retraining or fine-tuning
Comprehensive presentation with detailed proofs, per-class quantitative results, qualitative visualizations, and extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Overclaimed central contribution: title and abstract frame this as 'training-free MUAD' without clarifying that a strong pre-trained encoder (DiNOv3) is still required. This conflates pre-training with task-specific training and misleads readers about the method's true dependency on pre-trained models

Unfair baseline comparisons: Table 1 compares methods using different encoders (ResNet-50, DeiT, etc.) without standardizing backbone architectures. RAD's improvements may primarily reflect using a stronger frozen encoder rather than superior methodology

Loose theory-practice connection: the theoretical analysis (Section 2) focuses on why reconstruction-based methods fail, but the proposed method is retrieval-based. The theory doesn't explain why retrieval works better or provide insights into the retrieval approach itself

Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution—storing normal embeddings and computing anomaly scores via nearest-neighbor retrieval—is relatively straightforward, with multi-layer memory and spatial conditioning being engineering choices rather than conceptual innovations

Inadequate analysis of practical costs: storage requirements for multi-layer embeddings of all normal patches, retrieval latency for nearest-neighbor search, and scalability to large datasets are not thoroughly compared against training-based methods requiring only forward passes

Insufficient validation of theoretical assumptions: Assumption 2.1 (η-Lipschitz reconstruction) is not empirically verified for the specific architectures tested, weakening the theoretical justification for why the proposed method avoids these issues
Limited failure case analysis: qualitative visualizations show successful detections but few failure modes; weaker 3D-ADAM performance relative to 2D benchmarks lacks adequate explanation
Dataset-dependent hyperparameter tuning: neighborhood radius ρ and layer selection vary across datasets (Appendix A), suggesting per-dataset configuration despite the 'training-free' framing

strengths: Novel theoretical analysis of the fidelity-stability dilemma in encoder-decoder MUAD methods with rigorous mathematical proofs (Lemmas 2.1-2.2, Appendix C) showing fundamental trade-offs in reconstruction fidelity vs. stability
Strong and consistent empirical results across three major MUAD benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD) with particularly impressive few-shot performance, outperforming specialized few-shot methods
Practical training-free approach using frozen pre-trained encoders, eliminating task-specific training overhead and simplifying deployment

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple datasets, extensive ablation studies, data scaling analysis (Section 5.4), encoder quality impact (Section 5.5), and per-category quantitative results
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation, logical progression, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Multi-layer memory bank design that effectively captures multi-scale anomaly information from different encoder depths
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: retrieval-based approaches with memory banks are well-established; the main contribution is applying this to MUAD rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques
Modest performance improvements on standard benchmarks (0.4-2% in most cases), limiting practical significance despite statistical consistency

Significant practical limitations inadequately addressed: memory overhead for storing patch embeddings scales poorly with dataset size, inference latency from retrieval operations adds computational cost, authors acknowledge but defer solving these problems

Theoretical framework has gaps: Assumption 2.1 (local near-identity on benign directions) is strong; the connection between proving encoder-decoder failure and justifying retrieval success is implicit rather than explicit

Experimental comparisons may not be entirely fair: baselines use different protocols and datasets; frozen encoder assumption gives RAD advantage that other methods could also benefit from; limited discussion of performance attribution to pre-training vs. retrieval method

Limited dataset diversity: all three benchmarks focus on manufactured objects/textures; no evaluation on medical imaging, surveillance, or other critical MUAD domains; generalization beyond texture/object detection unclear

Incomplete failure case analysis: Section 6 briefly acknowledges limitations but provides insufficient analysis of when/why RAD underperforms; per-category variations significant but unexplained; 3D-ADAM results show larger gaps
Conditional 'training-free' claim: approach requires high-quality pre-trained encoders; practical advantage over fine-tuning-based approaches not clearly established

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework: The fidelity-stability dilemma for reconstruction-based methods is clearly formalized with rigorous mathematical analysis (Lemmas 2.2, Theorem D.3) providing insight into fundamental trade-offs in existing approaches.

Strong and comprehensive empirical results: State-of-the-art or competitive performance across four established benchmarks (MVTec-AD 99.7% I-AUROC, ViSA, Real-IAD, 3D-ADAM) with extensive ablation studies demonstrating clear contribution of each component.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Includes few-shot learning, data scaling analysis across different settings, encoder quality analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, and qualitative visualizations that substantially support the main claims.

Practical significance: Challenges the necessity of task-specific training, offering clear practical benefits (no domain-specific data/training overhead, natural class adaptation) with important implications for real-world deployment.

Multi-scale design with proper validation: The multi-layer memory bank with learned fusion weights (Eq. 10) elegantly captures semantics at different levels, validated through ablations showing +3.3% improvement from multi-layer alone.
Clear presentation: Well-structured writing, informative figures (especially Figure 2), and comprehensive appendix with full implementation details supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Individual components (multi-layer features, spatial conditioning, distance-based anomaly detection) are well-established techniques. The contribution is primarily in their combination and empirical validation rather than novel methodological innovation.

Restrictive theoretical assumptions: Assumption 2.1 (local near-identity reconstruction, Jacobian bounds) may not hold for all modern architectures. The theory is specific to reconstruction methods and doesn't explain why retrieval fundamentally avoids the identified dilemma—only why reconstruction is problematic.

Incomplete computational cost analysis: Retrieval requires distance computations to all stored embeddings, which could be expensive at scale. Memory overhead and inference latency comparisons are limited; claimed efficiency gains primarily relate to avoiding training rather than inference speedup.

Encoder selection favors the method: Using DINOv3 pre-trained encoder, while powerful, may disadvantage comparisons with methods designed for weaker encoders. While Appendix F addresses encoder quality, main results don't fully normalize for this factor.

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing reported. Unclear if results are single-run or averaged; small performance differences (e.g., 0.1% in Table 1) lack statistical validation.

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: The 3D-ADAM pixel-level F1 gap (46.4 vs 98.9 image-level) is attributed to class imbalance but not thoroughly investigated. Limited discussion of when and why RAD fails compared to alternatives.

Cross-dataset generalization unexplored: All evaluation uses benchmark datasets. No cross-dataset evaluation (e.g., trained on MVTec anomaly-free images, tested on ViSA anomalies) limits understanding of real-world generalization.

Memory bank scalability concerns: How performance scales with very large anomaly-free datasets remains unclear. Assumes anomaly-free features can be exhaustively stored, which may be impractical for large-scale applications.

Hyperparameter tuning despite 'training-free' claim: Despite avoiding model training, RAD requires tuning K, ρ, and layer-fusion weights. 'Training-free' primarily means task-specific model training only, not hyperparameter-free.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 benchmarks with strong image-level results and thorough ablation studies
Clear articulation of the fidelity-stability dilemma in reconstruction-based MUAD with rigorous mathematical analysis
Extensive supplementary experiments including data scaling, few-shot performance, encoder quality impact, and per-category results
Well-engineered system combining multi-layer memory banks with spatial conditioning and global context retrieval
Detailed proofs and theoretical analysis (Appendices C-D) providing formal justification for retrieval-based scoring
weaknesses: Core novelty is limited—retrieval-based and memory-based anomaly detection are well-established; the contribution is primarily engineering-focused rather than conceptually novel
Misleading 'training-free' framing: the method fundamentally relies on frozen ImageNet-pretrained encoders, making it task-specific training-dependent despite the claim
Severe computational overhead inadequately addressed: RAD is 6.5× slower than Dinomaly (293.7 vs 44.7 ms/image), a critical practical limitation largely dismissed
Significant pixel-level performance gap (46.4 vs 98.9 image-level F1 on 3D-ADAM) with concerning score overlap between normal and anomalous pixels (Table A4) unexplained
Weak theoretical motivation: Section 2's fidelity-stability analysis does not clearly explain why retrieval specifically solves this dilemma; the connection between diagnosis and solution is implicit
Arbitrary design choices (K=150, ρ values, fusion weights) lack principled justification; while ablations are provided, the paper offers limited guidance on setting these for new datasets
Unseen normal class generalization problem: RAD assigns low scores (0.0596 mean) to truly novel normal variations, with an ad-hoc fix that undermines the method's conceptual foundation

Presentation issues: dense mathematical notation, complex Figure 2, disconnected narrative between Section 2 analysis and Section 3 solution; 31 pages with extensive appendices make the paper difficult to assess
Marginal improvements over baselines given computational costs: image-level gains are often 1-3 percentage points while pixel-level improvements are inconsistent
Limited reproducibility guidance: no mentioned code availability, insufficient documentation for hyperparameter selection on new datasets, critical implementation details scattered across appendices

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution identifying and rigorously analyzing the fidelity-stability dilemma in reconstruction-based MUAD methods, with formal proofs provided in appendices
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art performance across four established benchmarks (MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, 3D-ADAM) with consistent improvements in image-level anomaly detection

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including extensive ablations, sensitivity analysis, few-shot scenarios, data scaling experiments, and per-category results demonstrating robustness across diverse object types
Practical training-free approach that eliminates task-specific training requirements, achieving efficiency gains and memory compression (32.6GB→0.37GB with minimal performance loss)
Well-motivated and technically sound framework combining multi-layer feature memory, global context-conditioned retrieval, and spatial conditioning in a principled manner
Clear presentation with thorough supplementary material covering implementation details, mathematical proofs, and extensive additional experiments (13 appendix sections)
Robust performance across challenging scenarios including few-shot detection, data scaling, and incremental class scaling, showing practical applicability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (memory banks, L2 distance matching, layer-wise fusion) are standard retrieval techniques; novelty lies primarily in their combination rather than fundamental innovations

Computational cost analysis inadequate: while O(K·P²) complexity stated, actual wall-clock timing comparisons with baselines missing; acknowledged latency overhead from retrieval operations not quantified

Scalability limitations for new categories: adding categories requires augmenting memory banks, contradicting somewhat the claim of flexible 'training-free' applicability; per-category memory grows as O(M·P)

Assumption 2.1 (local near-identity reconstruction condition) is specialized to encoder-decoder architectures; generalization to other paradigms unclear
Limited analysis of failure modes and anomaly types where method underperforms; missing discussion of domain transfer and fixed-threshold performance for practical deployment
